newsitem.title: FRANCE: French car sales seen down 10 pct in 1997 - Cofica.
newsitem.headline: French car sales seen down 10 pct in 1997 - Cofica.

text.p: French car sales are expected to fall around 10 percent next year, the car loan division of Compagnie Bancaire predicted on Thursday, echoing other gloomy forecasts for the industry.
Last week PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet said he expected the French car market to fall by nine to 10 percent next year to 1.93 million units.
Compagnie Bancaire's Cofica unit said it expected new car sales in France next year to total 1.89 million units, down from an estimated 2.1 million this year.

It attributed the anticipated drop to slow economic growth -- Cofica estimates France's gross domestic product will expand by 2.1 percent next year -- and the distorting effects of more than two years of state subsidies.

Excluding the effect of the rebates and the spillover into 1996 of late-1995 sales as a result of a three-week transport strike, the "natural" level of the French car market would have been 1.96 million units in 1996 instead of 2.1 million, he said.
The subsidies in the form of rebates pulled sales forward, leading to a surge in third-quarter sales ahead of their expiry at the end of September, and a plunge in orders since then.

"Carmakers are assuming the market will be catastrophic at least until the end of March," Vincent Becquey, the director of Cofica's car research division L'Observatoire de L'Automobile, told a news conference.
The economic environment is also expected to weigh on car sales in 1997. With inflation estimated at 1.9 percent next year in France, disposable income is expected to rise 1.5 percent, he said.
"This increase, while positive, is insufficient to maintain the market at the artificial levels of 1996," Becquey said.
He said one factor underpinning the market was a price war in France among manufacturers, who appear to be sacrificing profit margins in favour of increasing market share.
"Carmakers will battle each other even more fiercely in 1997 than they have in 1996," Becquey said.
While the outlook augurs poorly for carmakers' earnings, he said carmakers could sustain losses for some time, as they are not saddled with debt.

"It's altogether possible for French carmakers to take on debt and lose money on cars sold in France," he said. "The French car market has never been very profitable. Importers aren't earning much here either."

Sales of light commercial vehicles in France are expected to fall 7.5 percent next year to 305,000 units from around 330,000 in 1996, Becquey said, attributing the slump to weak growth in new businesses -- the driving force for that segment.
Renault SA and the French carmakers association CCFA have not yet issued their 1997 forecasts.
